definition: Sequential, depth-first reasoning in which each inference is justified by the last - the discipline behind a rigorous differential diagnosis - as opposed to lateral thinking, which sidesteps to new frames.
example: Working vertically from raised troponin to mechanism, she ruled out each alternative before widening the search.

definition: A ranked list of the conditions that could explain a patient's findings, narrowed by history, examination and tests.
example: Chest pain has a differential that runs from reflux to pulmonary embolism.

definition: A drug class that mimics the gut hormone glucagon-like peptide-1 to raise insulin release, slow gastric emptying and reduce appetite; used in type 2 diabetes and obesity.
A single number that sums the small effects of many genetic variants to estimate a person's inherited susceptibility to a disease.
A blood test that detects tumour-derived DNA or cells, enabling cancer screening and monitoring without surgical tissue sampling.
A CRISPR-derived technique that chemically converts one DNA letter to another without cutting both strands of the double helix.
A miniature, simplified organ grown in the lab from stem cells that reproduces some structure and function of the real tissue.
An approach that pairs a diagnostic imaging agent with a matching therapeutic one that targets the same molecular marker.
The study of how a person's genes influence their response to drugs, used to choose agents and doses.
A computational model of a patient or organ, updated with real data, used to simulate how a treatment might perform.
Software that listens to a consultation and drafts the clinical note automatically for the clinician to review.
A model that delivers acute, hospital-level care in the patient's own residence, supported by remote monitoring and visiting staff.
A programme of exercise, nutrition and psychological preparation undertaken before an operation to improve recovery.
An evidence-based perioperative pathway - early feeding, opioid-sparing analgesia, early mobilisation - that shortens recovery and reduces complications.
Surgery in which the operator controls instruments through a console, gaining tremor filtering, magnified 3D vision and articulated wrists.
Surgery performed by a surgeon who is geographically distant from the patient, using robotic systems and low-latency networks.
Transplanting living cells, tissues or organs from one species into another, such as gene-edited pig kidneys into humans.
A compound that selectively clears senescent ('zombie') cells, investigated as a way to delay age-related disease.
A biomarker that estimates biological age from chemical (methylation) patterns on DNA rather than from years lived.
The number of patients who must receive an intervention for one additional patient to benefit, compared with control.
The tendency to lock onto an early diagnostic impression and under-weight evidence that contradicts it.
Accepting a diagnosis before it has been fully verified, so that other possibilities are never considered.
Real-time electrophysiological monitoring of nerves and the spinal cord during an operation to prevent injury.
